planting.note: Set out container divisions in spring or early fall into moist, strongly acidic, humus-rich soil beneath deciduous or conifer shade; this selection establishes slowly and should not be grown from seed if heavy fruiting is the goal.

directions: Very Berry is a heavily-fruiting selection of the native eastern wintergreen, chosen for producing noticeably larger and more numerous pea-sized red berries than typical wild-collected plants. It forms a low evergreen mat of glossy, aromatic leaves that bronze-purple in cold weather, spreading slowly by rhizomes to knit together a woodland groundcover over several seasons. Give it the same acidic, moisture-retentive soil favored by rhododendrons and mountain laurel, and avoid lime or neutral-pH sites where it will decline. The persistent winter berries are a reliable food source for grouse, turkey, and other wildlife, and both berries and foliage retain the classic wintergreen (methyl salicylate) fragrance when crushed.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant nursery divisions in spring into moist, acidic, well-drained woodland soil in part to full shade; this patented sport is propagated only by cuttings or tissue culture, never by seed.

directions: Peppermint Pearl is a patented sport of the native eastern wintergreen (cultivar 'SPECGP11', bred by Special Plant Zundert B.V. in the Netherlands) distinguished by its persistent white berries in place of the species' usual bright red, giving a frosty, peppermint-candy look against the glossy dark evergreen foliage. Small bell-shaped white flowers open in early summer and are followed by the large waxy berries that hold on the plant from fall into the following spring. It spreads gradually into a dense, weed-suppressing mat and needs the same acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist conditions as other ericaceous woodland natives. Use it as an underplanting beneath azaleas or conifers where its unusual berry color provides a point of contrast through the dormant season.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil; this coralberry tolerates part shade and poor urban soils and needs no special amendment.

directions: Proud Berry Pink is a patented coralberry selection (cultivar 'Sofie', discovered by Catharina Marie Hoekstra-Arisz in Beverwijk, the Netherlands) grown for its unusually large, bright pink-tinged-white berries that weigh down long arching stems from late summer through winter, well after the small bell-shaped flowers fade. Blue-green, rounded leaves give a clean backdrop to the fruit display, and the neat branching habit holds its shape without the legginess of older snowberry types. It adapts readily to clay, poor fill, and part-shade foundation plantings, and deer generally leave it alone. Cut stems with fruit clusters attached make long-lasting additions to fall and winter arrangements.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial shade; this dwarf selection fits foundation plantings and smaller woodland gardens where the full-size species would outgrow the space.

directions: Taylor's Treasure is a compact, naturally dwarf selection of Florida leucothoe discovered as a seedling by David W. Taylor at Taylor's Nursery in Semmes, Alabama, in 1995, and sold under the trade name Leprechaun. It keeps the species' graceful arching habit and fragrant, urn-shaped white flower clusters in mid-spring to early summer, but on a denser plant with smaller, narrower leaves that emerge tinged with copper before maturing glossy dark green. It is substantially more compact than wild-type Florida leucothoe, making it easier to use as a specimen or informal low screen in shaded Deep South gardens. Grow it in the same moist, acidic, well-drained woodland conditions as azaleas and camellias, sheltered from harsh afternoon sun and drying wind.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average to moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; foliage color is most intense with a few hours of morning sun and some afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: Red Zeppelin is a recent Proven Winners ColorChoice sweetshrub introduction grown primarily for its lustrous, deep burgundy-purple foliage, which holds its dark color on both leaf surfaces through the entire growing season rather than fading to green like most purple-leaved shrubs. The maroon, strap-petaled flowers open in late spring to early summer against the dark leaves, giving strong contrast even though the fragrance is lighter than some older sweetshrub selections. Its compact, well-branched, rounded habit makes it easier to place in a mixed shrub border or woodland-edge planting than straight-species sweetshrub, which can become loose and suckering with age. Like the native species, it is adaptable to clay and average garden soil as long as drainage is reasonable, and it tolerates the partial shade of a woodland edge without losing leaf color.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in average, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this selection was bred for reliable fall color across a range of growing conditions.

directions: Plum Pudding is a University of Connecticut NativeStar introduction of the native arrowwood viburnum, bred by Mark Brand and Jessica Lubell-Brand and selected for consistently producing burgundy-red fall foliage even in sites where straight-species arrowwood often colors unevenly or stays green. Flat clusters of small white flowers cover the dense, full-habited shrub in late spring, drawing pollinators, and are followed by blue-black drupes that birds strip quickly in fall. It tolerates wet or dry soil, heavy clay, and juglone from nearby black walnuts, making it a dependable choice for naturalistic mass plantings, hedgerows, and rain gardens. Give it part shade to full sun; flowering and fall color are both best with at least a half day of direct sun.
sources: HortScience vol. 61 (2026), 'Plum Pudding and Raisinette: Two New Native Viburnum Cultivars'

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to average, acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; this compact selection suits smaller gardens where full-size witherod viburnum would be too large.

directions: Raisinette is a University of Connecticut NativeStar selection of witherod viburnum, released alongside 'Plum Pudding' and bred for a compact, densely branching habit noticeably shorter than wild-type plants, making it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller shrub borders. Spring growth emerges with a pronounced, synchronous bronze flush before maturing to clean green, and profuse flat-topped white flower clusters in late spring give way to the species' signature multicolor pink-to-blue-to-black fruit clusters that ripen unevenly for a long season of interest. Fall foliage turns a strong crimson, adding a second season of color to the berry display. It tolerates wet soils and part shade better than most viburnums, making it useful along pond edges, in rain gardens, or at a woodland margin.
sources: HortScience vol. 61 (2026), 'Plum Pudding and Raisinette: Two New Native Viburnum Cultivars'
